extracted.intended_audience: orators, rhetoricians, forensic advocates, and students of classical rhetoric
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for composing harmonious, persuasive prose (periodic sentences) for oratory — how to use metrical 'numbers', cadence, word-order, and sentence divisions to please the ear without lapsing into verse. Emphasises when and how to employ measured or 'numerous' style in forensic (legal/political) contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-chosen words and harmonious numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two things which give a relish to our language,--well-chosen words, and harmonious numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Words are the materials of language; number smooths and polishes them. Aim for both good diction and an underlying cadence so that the ear receives pleasure while the meaning is conveyed. Example contrast: raw, unmeasured language vs. polished, numerous style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of numbers (prosaic metre) in prose
rubrics_metrics.description: Prose is susceptible of numbers, and the numbers of an Orator must be the same as those of a Poet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat 'numbers' (combinations of long and short syllables) as tools to regulate flow, strength, and pauses of a period. Numbers are not decorative alone but give the period its force; they should be present though not as rigidly arranged as in verse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blend and diversify feet (avoid exclusive repetition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Our language should be intermingled and diversified with all the varieties of number; should we confine ourselves to any particular feet, it would be impossible to escape the censure of the hearer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promiscuously employ different feet (iambic, dactyl, paeon, spondee, etc.). Anti-pattern: sticking to one foot (e.g., continuous iambics or dactyls) risks producing verse-like uniformity or listener censure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer the paeon as principal ingredient
rubrics_metrics.description: Our style ... should abound most in the paeon (so much recommended by the excellent author above-mentioned) though still in conjunction with many other feet which he entirely omits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the paeon frequently as a medium between common talk and lofty verse; but do not exclude other feet. The paeon is useful for maintaining dignity without sounding poetic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match foot choice to subject and tone
rubrics_metrics.description: The iambic should be the leading number in those subjects which require a plain and simple style; the paeon in such as require more compass and elevation; and the dactyl is equally applicable to both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select feet to suit purpose: iambic ≈ conversational/plain; paeon ≈ elevated/dignified; dactyl ≈ pomp or emphasis. Blend as occasion demands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid prose becoming verse — do not be exactly measured
rubrics_metrics.description: Our numbers are not to be so conspicuous in prose as in verse; ... if our language neither limps nor fluctuates, but keeps an even and a steady pace, it is sufficiently 'numerous'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not adopt the invariable, regular beats of poetry. Exact number (as in poetry) is a fault in prose; aim for the appearance of natural flow while retaining musicality. Anti-pattern: composing prose with fixed, poem-like beats ('to compose a poem').

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulate cadence across whole period, not only the end
rubrics_metrics.description: It is true that the ear always directs its view to the close of a sentence... but the whole compass of our periods ought likewise to be regulated, and not totally neglected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attend to beginning, middle, and end so the sentence runs freely and corresponds to its conclusion. The cadence should feel purposeful from the start; don't only aim for a good closing cadence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolve sentence termination from the beginning
rubrics_metrics.description: It will be necessary at the very beginning of a sentence, to resolve upon the manner in which you would have it terminate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose (or when speaking extempore, mentally form) the period in advance so words and order lead naturally to the intended close. This planning helps keep middle and end congruent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ commas and colons (commas/colons/periods) as rhetorical units
rubrics_metrics.description: To speak in 'commas' and 'colons' ... in real causes, should occupy the major part of an Oration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure sentences into members (commas = short member, colon = longer member, period = full sentence). Use rapid short members for forceful, close-fighting passages; use colons and full periods for dignified, ornate passages. Vary member types to avoid monotony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use numerous (measured) style sparingly and in specific contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: A numerous style may be properly employed, either when anything is to be commended in a free and ornamental manner ... when a narrative is to be delivered which requires more dignity than pathos ... or when a material circumstance is to be amplified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve strongly measured prose for praise, elevated narrative, amplification, and perorations after you have secured the audience's goodwill. Overuse will reveal artifice and tire the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not continue a measured flow too long
rubrics_metrics.description: This measured and numerous flow of language is never to be continued too long ... except in the cases above-mentioned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit stretches of elaborate cadence. In forensic oratory especially, confine numerous style to suitable clauses (commas and colons) to avoid satiety, destroying pathos, or revealing artifice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid frequent repetition of the same cadence (e.g., dichoree)
rubrics_metrics.description: In prosaic numbers nothing can be more faulty than a continued or frequent repetition of the same cadence: as the 'dichoree', therefore, is a very sonorous number, we should be the more sparing in the use of it, to prevent a satiety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vary cadences; repeating a distinctive cadence or foot quickly leads to listener boredom and exposes the craft behind the language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use short feet for spirited rapid style; long feet for sober, sedate style
rubrics_metrics.description: Our numbers will advance more rapidly by the use of short feet, and more coolly and sedately by the use of long ones. The former are best adapted to a warm and spirited style, and the latter to sober narratives and explanations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose foot length to control pacing: short feet accelerate, long feet slow and add dignity. Apply this to match emotional tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select appropriate closing feet (cretic, paeon, spondee, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: The cretic ... and its companion the paeon ... is reckoned a proper and a very useful ingredient in harmonious prose ... the sober spondee ... has yet a firm and steady step, which gives it an air of dignity, and especially in the comma and the colon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer cretic or paeon for sentence closings; use spondees for weight in commas/colons. Be aware that the last syllable's length is often immaterial. Avoid trochee at period end (short final syllable) as less agreeable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Juncture and concinnity (composition) matter besides numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: The harmony of language does not result entirely from the use of 'numbers', but from the 'juncture' and 'composition' of our words; and from that neatness and 'concinnity' of expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft word-order and sound relationships (e.g., vowel-consonant succession, euphony) so that mere arrangement produces agreeable sound independent of metrical feet. Example: alternating word endings and beginnings to produce smooth sound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ rhetorical devices (parallelism, contrast, repeated endings) to produce cadence
rubrics_metrics.description: When parallel circumstances are compared, or opposite ones contrasted, or words of the same termination are placed in a regular succession, they seldom fail to produce a numerous cadence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use structured grammatical and semantic patterns — parallel clauses, antithesis, epistrophe, etc. — to create cadence and musicality without strictly metrical feet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt period length and member counts to audience's ear
rubrics_metrics.description: A full period ... is generally composed of four parts ... But it sometimes ... happens, that a sentence either falls short of, or exceeds the limits of a regular period, to prevent it from fatiguing the ear on the one hand, or disappointing it on the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for an agreeable mediocrity: neither too long nor too short. Use four-member periods often, but adjust to avoid fatigue or underwhelming closure. The audience's capacity and attention determine ideal length.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use short, punchy members for forensic 'close-fighting'
rubrics_metrics.description: For those sentences which are to be used like daggers for close-fighting, their very shortness makes our numbers less exceptionable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In argumentative rebuttals or emphatic attacks, prefer very short commas/colons (two or three words) to deliver rapid, staccato blows that are effective and less likely to appear metrically contrived.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numbers should gratify the ear without drawing attention
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing should be so numerous in reality as that which appears to be least so, and yet has a forcible effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for invisible craftsmanship: the listener should admire sentiments and words and unconsciously enjoy cadence, not detect the metre. If listeners notice the craft, it risks disgust or parody.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let the ear be the final arbiter
rubrics_metrics.description: The ear alone, without the assistance of art, can determine its limits by the natural powers of sensation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use rules as guides but trust auditory judgement in context. Practice and listening will cultivate the sensibility to know when cadence is pleasing or forced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify and vary word-choices: metaphorical, new-coined, antique
rubrics_metrics.description: The words also in each may be divided into three classes,--the metaphorical, the new-coined, and the antique;--for at present we have no concern with words proper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manage lexical register: poets may use tropes and archaic or novel coinages more freely; orators should balance metaphorical, neologistic, and archaic words for effect, reserving extremes for suitable contexts.
